blocks.text: A class is more than a group of fields. It is a promise about which combinations of those fields callers can encounter. HarborWorks represents completion as a percentage. The meaning is not “whatever integer happens to be stored”; it is an integer in the inclusive range zero through one hundred. A useful class prevents callers from accidentally turning that promise into a comment that no code enforces.

blocks.text: The harder case is an invariant involving several members. A report window might require first <= last, or a dataset might require a unique identifier for every row. Validating each field independently does not establish either relationship. Think in terms of accepted states and permitted transitions. The interface should expose the transitions the application needs while withholding arbitrary representation edits.

blocks.text: Some domains need an empty or unavailable state. Model that state explicitly, perhaps through an optional value, rather than selecting an out-of-range sentinel and hoping every operation remembers it. A representation with fewer hidden states often produces simpler tests and fewer exceptional branches.

blocks.text: Write the invariant before writing the constructor. For a percentage, the accepted set is small and explicit. Zero means a valid starting point; one hundred means complete; neither should be repurposed as an error sentinel. A negative input is not an incomplete percentage but an invalid candidate. That distinction determines whether construction throws, returns a typed error through a factory, or applies a deliberately documented conversion policy.

blocks.text: The constructor and setter should use the same validation rule. Duplicated validation tends to drift: one path accepts one hundred while another accidentally excludes it. A private validation helper returning the accepted integer lets both operations share the boundary test. It also makes the setter’s order obvious: validate first, then assign. A failed validation leaves the stored value unchanged because mutation has not begun.

A failed validation leaves the stored value unchanged because mutation has not begun.

blocks.text: Validation must cover the actual type. For floating-point percentages, comparisons alone need thought about non-finite values such as NaN. For an integer percentage, that issue does not exist, but representability can still matter at a parsing boundary. Do not parse a huge external number into a narrow type and assume the class can recover the intended value afterward. Parsing and domain validation are separate gates: first establish a representable integer, then establish a valid percentage.

blocks.text: The constructor’s guarantee is about successful construction. If it rejects a candidate by throwing, no complete percentage object is returned. The calling code should not expect to inspect a partially valid instance. Later RAII examples explain what happens to already-constructed members when a larger object’s construction fails.

blocks.text: Coupled state deserves a combined update operation. Suppose a date interval exposes set_first and set_last, each requiring a valid interval immediately afterward. Moving the interval from one disjoint range to another can become awkward or impossible through the intermediate states. A single replace_interval(first, last) operation can validate a candidate pair and commit it together. This is a small transaction, even though no database is involved.

blocks.text: Avoid returning a mutable container when the class promises unique IDs or sorted data. An unrestricted std::vector<Record>& lets callers erase, duplicate, or reorder elements without passing the invariant checks. A read-only query, a copied snapshot, an iterator range with a documented borrowing period, or a domain-specific mutation may be a better fit. Each has different costs and lifetime rules; choose deliberately rather than exposing the representation simply because it is convenient during early development.

blocks.text: A const member function treats the object through a const-qualified access path. It is useful for queries such as size() const or value() const because callers can use them on const objects and understand that ordinary direct mutation is not part of the interface. It is not a universal promise that the outside world stays unchanged. The function could write a log, inspect a clock, or modify an object reached through a pointer member.

blocks.text: This distinction is especially important with containers of owning pointers. A const container prevents replacing its pointer elements through that container interface, but it does not necessarily make each pointee const. For a deeply read-only public model, the pointee type or the exposed interface must express that requirement too. Constness follows types and access paths; it is not an invisible recursive freeze operation.

A percentage class does not need a mutable integer reference because any integer mutation must be validated. The same language facility is therefore appropriate for one abstraction and inappropriate for another.

blocks.text: Parameter design should reflect use. Small arithmetic values are usually straightforward by-value parameters. A large object inspected only during the call can often be borrowed by const reference. A value that the callee will store can be accepted by value and moved into a member, allowing callers to choose copying or transfer at the call site. These are defaults to evaluate, not laws that eliminate measurement or domain reasoning.

blocks.text: Consider Readings(std::vector<int> values). When the caller supplies an lvalue, a copy constructs the parameter and the constructor can then move its storage into the member. When the caller supplies a suitable rvalue, ownership can be transferred into the parameter and then into the member. The extra move is usually a small operation for the default vector representation, but the exact costs depend on the participating type and allocator. Chapter 5 examines the distinction in detail.

blocks.text: A const reference parameter can bind to a temporary for the duration of a call, but storing that reference as a member does not grant the temporary a new lifetime. A constructor that retains a borrowed vector must require an owner that outlives the constructed object, and its name or documentation should make that requirement visible. For an ordinary readings value, owning the vector is easier to reason about than making every caller manage an invisible lifetime dependency.

blocks.text: The Rule of Zero works because member types already provide appropriate resource operations. A string owns its character sequence; a vector owns its elements and storage. Their enclosing class can rely on member destruction and memberwise copying when those actions match the class’s intended semantics. Removing an unnecessary destructor is not merely a style preference: it avoids accidentally suppressing an implicitly generated move operation.

blocks.text: Memberwise behavior must still be reviewed. A class storing both a vector and a pointer into that vector has a relationship that memberwise copying does not automatically repair. The copied pointer may still designate the original vector. Likewise, a class storing an owned sequence and a cached count can have a broken moved-from relationship if the sequence becomes empty but the cached scalar does not change. Prefer representations that do not duplicate derivable facts when that makes the invariant simpler.

blocks.text: Rule-of-Zero design is therefore a representation choice, not a command to ignore special members forever. If the class genuinely has a native exclusive handle, put that handle inside an appropriate RAII member. If copying the wrapper would not make sense, let that member make copying unavailable. The public class then follows its real ownership policy without maintaining a second, parallel cleanup implementation.

topics.summary: A destructor added merely to call a member’s destructor is wrong; members are already destroyed automatically. blocks.text: Review the class whenever a new member changes its ownership role. A raw pointer observer may be fine if its lifetime contract is explicit, but a raw owning handle changes the special-member problem. The correct response may be to wrap that handle in a dedicated RAII type, restoring Rule-of-Zero composition at the application level.

blocks.text: Before deleting custom special members, record the behavior the class currently promises. Does copying create independent values? Is copying prohibited? Is a moved-from object allowed to be empty? Is assignment required to preserve the old state if allocation fails? Different answers can require different representations even when both versions use standard-library members.

Different answers can require different representations even when both versions use standard-library members.

blocks.text: A hand-written copy loop may conceal a defect that a vector member removes. Conversely, a generated copy operation may copy a reference member so that two objects borrow the same external service. That may be intentional for a reporter but wrong for an independently owned dataset. “Compiler-generated” means the language supplies memberwise operations under its rules; it does not mean the domain design has been approved.

blocks.text: Use compile-time checks to document the selected capabilities where useful. Type traits can show whether a type is copy-constructible or nothrow-move-constructible. Runtime checks should then verify the observable consequences: independent edits, preserved invariants after rejection, and correct empty-state behavior. Neither kind of test replaces the other. A trait can be true for a type whose copy operation implements the wrong application semantics.

blocks.text: A vector-owning class normally needs no custom destructor or copy implementation. A native owning handle requires a cleanup policy, usually isolated in an RAII member. Const qualification narrows permitted operations but does not make shared external state immutable or synchronized.

blocks.text: Engineering takeaway. Preserve one invariant through every entry point, and let well-designed members manage their own resources.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: A valid public state is stronger than a private field. The interval’s invariant belongs to the pair of endpoints, so its update boundary should cover the pair. The percentage’s setter preserves the old value because validation precedes mutation, not because an exception magically rolls changes back. A Rule-of-Zero representation reduces ownership code only when the members’ copy and move behavior matches the enclosing class’s meaning.
